task: search for an apartment and contact the listing (Zillow, Apartments.com, Trulia): set location, price, and bedroom filters, evaluate listings and their trustworthiness, pick candidates, send an inquiry or tour request; complete when the inquiry-sent or tour-request confirmation is on screen. Surface pinned: an apartment-listing website or app. Variants: submitting a rental application with documents, roommate finding, and buying a home do not belong.

tree.label: Find a rental apartment
tree.note: do 1. 2 only as the account state demands - 9tEl registers before anything else, most keepers arrive signed in and skip it, and 8.2 reaches into 2.5 when a save hits the login wall (dS5q). repeat 3, 4, and 5 in any order until the results fit: 5.1's count drives the revisions (9tEl, mKVE, n9qo), and 3.4 or 3.5 re-cut the set as silently as any filter. 5.6 opens 6 - except on 3.3, which lands inside 6 directly and reaches 5 only by backing out (iHOh). from 6: back to 5 for the next candidate (pCy8, mKVE, Q8ex), into 7 to prepare contact, into 8 to keep it - in any order, or not at all. no keeper carries 7 past 7.5. 8.6 and 8.7 close the loop on 8's own actions.

children.label: Reach the rental search
children.note: 1.1 then 1.2. 1.3 whenever the platform lands on the for-sale side - at entry (4NIC, XmWM), inside the search sheet (7oPn), or as a check that finds nothing wrong (n9qo). 1.4 and 1.5 as they come up.

questions.question: Is the result about to be opened the official Zillow site rather than a sponsored ad or a third-party lookalike?
questions.why: Selecting the top result titled 'Zillow: Real Estate, Apartments, Mortgages & Home Values' ensures you navigate to the legitimate platform rather than a sponsored ad or third-party site.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to verify they are entering the authentic, secure real estate marketplace rather than a potentially deceptive link.
questions.check: Which search results carry an Ad or Sponsored label, and which one is the official site?
questions.say_example: Skipped 2 sponsored results and opened zillow.com.

questions.question: Which option under the Rent menu matches the ask?
questions.why: The 'Rent' dropdown menu offers different starting points like apartments, houses, or all rentals, which sets the baseline property filter for your search.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to immediately narrow the search strictly to apartments instead of having to sift through single-family homes and other property types.
questions.check: Which options does the Rent menu list, and which is selected?
questions.say_example: Opened the Rent menu and picked apartments.

questions.question: Are the search results showing rentals for your chosen zip code?
questions.why: The screen displays '[address] Listings' and an active 'For Rent' filter, which confirms the base search parameters are correct before you add more specific filters.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to visually confirm that the agent is searching in the correct area and hasn't accidentally included properties for sale.
questions.check: What area and listing type does the results header show?
questions.say_example: The results are for <downtown Seattle>, and you asked for <Capitol Hill>. Redoing the search.

questions.question: Is the search set to For rent or For sale?
questions.why: The interface defaults to the 'For sale' tab, which will show homes to buy instead of apartments to lease if left unchanged.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to verify that the fundamental search category matches their specific housing needs.
questions.check: Which tab is active, For rent or For sale?
questions.say_example: The site loaded homes for sale. You want rentals. I switched the tab to For rent.

questions.question: A notice is covering the results and it changes how the price is read - what does it say, before it is dismissed?
questions.why: The site is displaying a 'Say hello to total monthly price' modal that overlays the 26,075 available Los Angeles rentals and needs to be cleared to interact with the page.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to read and understand how the platform calculates and displays the total monthly price before the notice is dismissed.
questions.check: Is a popup or modal overlaying the results?
questions.say_example: Closed the total monthly price popup.

questions.question: What language is the site set to?
questions.why: The dropdown menu displays multiple language options like Español and 简体中文, which determines the language used for the search interface and listing details.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: If the agent defaults to English without asking, you lose the opportunity to navigate the site and read apartment details in your preferred language.
questions.check: Which language is selected in the site's language menu?
questions.say_example: The site came up in <Spanish>. I switched it to English.

children.label: Sign in or register
children.note: 2.1; 2.2 to 2.4 only on a first run (9tEl). 2.5 fires mid-task, entered from 8.2, when a save demands an account (dS5q). most keepers arrive signed in and the whole goal is a no-op.

questions.question: Does the page show an account already signed in?
questions.why: The narrator tells you to create an account, but the profile name '[name]' is already visible in the top right corner.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses time and risks account duplication if the agent blindly attempts to sign up instead of using the active session.
questions.check: Does the page header show a signed-in account name?
questions.say_example: You're already signed in as <[name]>, so I'm skipping the sign-up.

questions.question: How do you want to sign up for an account?
questions.why: The homepage provides options to either fill out your information manually or use a third-party service like Google, Facebook, or Apple to create an account.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide whether to link your existing social profiles to the apartment platform or keep them separate with a manual login.
questions.check: What sign-in options does the page offer?
questions.say_example: The site wants an account before I can send anything. I can sign up with your email, or with your Google. Which one?

questions.question: What password should you set for the new account, or should you skip it?
questions.why: The screen requires choosing between entering an 8-15 character password to save the account or clicking 'Do this later'.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to choose their own security credentials or opt out of creating a permanent account.
questions.check: Does the password screen offer a skip option, and what are the password rules?
questions.say_example: It's asking to set a password. There's a skip button. Skip it, or set one now?

questions.question: Do you want Google Chrome to save your password for Trulia?
questions.why: The browser displayed a prompt asking whether to save the password for Trulia.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to decide whether their login credentials are saved in the browser's password manager.
questions.check: Is the browser showing a save-password prompt?
questions.say_example: Chrome offered to save the password. I said no.

questions.question: Does the page say the email must be verified before inquiries are delivered?
questions.why: The browser tab shows a 'Welcome! Please verify your e[mail]' notification, which might be required for the platform to actually deliver your messages to landlords.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user's inquiries might be silently blocked or flagged as spam by the platform because their account email was never verified.
questions.check: Does the page or tab show a verify-your-email notice?
questions.say_example: The site says to verify your email first. Until then your messages may not reach anyone. I'll open the email and click the link.

children.label: Set the search area
children.note: one of 3.1, 3.2, or 3.3 fixes the place - 3.3 skips the results stage entirely (iHOh). 3.4 and 3.5 any time after results exist; both change the result set silently, so 5.1 is re-read after them.

questions.question: What search radius is set?
questions.why: The search interface includes an 'area' radius slider (e.g., '0 km'), allowing you to strictly limit results to the exact city or expand the search to surrounding suburbs.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to control the geographic strictness of your search, potentially missing out on nearby options if the radius is too tight, or seeing irrelevant listings if it is too broad.
questions.check: What is the search radius set to?
questions.say_example: Search radius left at 0 km, exact city only.

questions.question: Where exactly do you want to search for an apartment?
questions.why: The search bar prompts for an address, neighborhood, city, or ZIP code to focus the results on the exact area you want to live.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: If an agent decides the search area, they might pick a broader city search instead of the specific neighborhood or zip code you actually want to live in.
questions.check: What location is entered in the search bar?
questions.say_example: What area should I search? A city, a neighborhood, or a zip code all work.

questions.question: Which suggestion is the place you meant?
questions.why: Typing 'bos' generated a dropdown list of multiple cities like 'Boston, MA' and 'Bossier City, LA', requiring a specific selection to center the search map.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to specify the exact target city or neighborhood they want to explore for apartments.
questions.check: What suggestions does the location dropdown list?
questions.say_example: There's more than one <Portland>. I'll use <Portland, Oregon>. OK, or did you mean <Maine>?

questions.question: What location is set for the search?
questions.why: The screen shows the location tag 'All Upper East Side', which dictates the geographic boundaries for all the apartment listings you will see.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to decide exactly how broad or narrow the neighborhood boundaries should be for your new home.
questions.check: What location tag does the page show applied?
questions.say_example: Searching <the Upper East Side>, rentals only.

questions.question: Did the map actually load the correct city and state, or did it default to a different city with the same name?
questions.why: Many cities share names across different states or countries (e.g., Portland, OR vs. Portland, ME). If the search executes without explicitly selecting a state, the site might load the wrong geographical area.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent wastes time searching and filtering apartments in completely the wrong state, returning useless results.
questions.check: What city and state does the results header or map label show?
questions.say_example: Heads up, the map loaded <Portland, Maine>, and you wanted <Oregon>. Fixing it.

questions.question: Should you resume a previous search from the dropdown or start a new one?
questions.why: The search bar dropdown displays your recent viewing history and previous searches, offering a quick way to continue where you left off instead of typing a new location.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might automatically type in a new location, ignoring your recent search history and missing the context of what you were previously interested in.
questions.check: What recent searches does the dropdown show?
questions.say_example: Started fresh, didn't reuse the old search.

questions.question: The red banner says the addresses could not be found - is the search failing on the site's address format, not on there being no such buildings?
questions.why: The screen showed a red error banner stating the addresses could not be found, requiring you to remove the city name to make the search work.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the awareness of the site's specific address formatting quirks needed to successfully search for specific buildings.
questions.check: Does the page show an address-not-found error?
questions.say_example: The site couldn't find that address. I'm trying it again without the city name.

questions.question: Did the site change the address you typed?
questions.why: The input field updated from '[address] 42nd st' to '[address] 42nd Street, N' and showed results for 'Silver Towers', indicating the site altered your specific search.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to notice the address auto-correction and determine if the substituted building is an acceptable alternative to your original target.
questions.check: Does the executed search text match what was typed?
questions.say_example: The site changed the address to <Silver Towers on 42nd Street>. That may be a different building than yours. Checking before I go on.

questions.question: Is the boundary still applied after the removal?
questions.why: The screen at 1:26 shows the Seattle boundary outline and the 'Remove Boundary' button are still present, contradicting the claim that the boundary was removed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses an accurate understanding of how many rentals are actually available within their specific desired area.
questions.check: Are the boundary outline and Remove Boundary button still shown?
questions.say_example: The boundary didn't actually clear. I'm removing it again.

questions.question: Is the listing status filter set to available listings?
questions.why: The screen shows a typo in the custom boundary name ('Union Squarea') and the listing status is set to include only unavailable listings.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to find an actual apartment because the agent wastes time searching for unavailable properties in a misspelled location.
questions.check: What listing status is the search set to?
questions.say_example: The status filter was set to homes already taken. I switched it to available ones.

questions.question: Did the map silently clear your custom drawn boundary when you applied a new filter?
questions.why: On some sites, applying a new filter like price or bedrooms causes the map to refresh and silently erase any custom boundaries you previously drew.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user receives listings outside their desired neighborhood because the agent didn't notice the custom boundary was dropped.
questions.check: Is the drawn boundary still applied after the filter change?
questions.say_example: Adding the price filter quietly erased the map boundary. I'm drawing it again.

children.label: Set the filters
children.note: any subset, any order - the dominant pattern is opening a menu and changing nothing (five Zillow keepers change zero filters). 4.8 ends every menu, and whether the choices took effect only shows in 5.1's count. 4.9 where ordering matters. re-entered whenever 5.1 reads too many, too few, or zero.

questions.question: Is the accepts-applications filter selected?
questions.why: Selecting the option for listings that accept Zillow applications can streamline the rental process if you are ready to apply.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to decide if the convenience of applying directly through the platform outweighs potentially missing out on other good listings.
questions.check: Does the filter panel offer an accepts-applications option, and is it selected?
questions.say_example: Left the accepts-applications-on-the-site filter off.

questions.question: Which of the asked-for filters are set?
questions.why: The 'More Filters' menu contains options for move-in dates and specific amenities needed to match the requested preferences.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You risk wasting time inquiring about apartments that do not meet your specific move-in timeline or amenity requirements.
questions.check: Which filters does the panel show selected?
questions.say_example: Setting your filters now. Move-in <June 1>, cats OK, laundry in the unit, parking.

questions.question: Are commute or transit filters set?
questions.why: The screen displays unused commute and transit filters next to the search button, which could help narrow down the results to locations that fit your daily travel needs.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to ensure the resulting apartments are conveniently located for your specific daily commute or public transit needs.
questions.check: Does the page offer commute or transit filters, and are they set?
questions.say_example: Commute filter available, not used.

questions.question: Which floor options are selected?
questions.why: The screen provides specific floor checkboxes like 'EC', '1', '2', and '3' to help narrow down the search based on accessibility or living preferences.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this choice means the agent might include undesirable floor levels that do not match your personal living or accessibility needs.
questions.check: Which floor options are checked?
questions.say_example: No floor preference set.

questions.question: What maximum square footage is set?
questions.why: The screen showed a dropdown for the maximum square foot range to filter out apartments that are too large.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The person loses the ability to cap the apartment size, potentially leading to recommendations that are unnecessarily large.
questions.check: What maximum size is selected?
questions.say_example: No size cap set.

questions.question: Which buildings and listing statuses are set in the filters?
questions.why: The screen provides inputs for specific building addresses and a dropdown for listing status to help narrow the search to truly available units.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to target their specific preferred buildings and apply their nuanced understanding of how local management companies classify off-market units.
questions.check: What building and status inputs are set?
questions.say_example: Building and status inputs left on the defaults.

questions.question: What year-built range is set?
questions.why: The 'More Filters' menu includes a 'Year built' range, allowing you to restrict your search to newer constructions or historic buildings.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to filter out older buildings that might lack modern insulation or amenities, or conversely, to seek out historic charm.
questions.check: What year-built range is set?
questions.say_example: Year-built filter not used.

questions.question: What price range should you set to stay within your budget?
questions.why: The 'Price Range' popover allows you to input specific minimum and maximum values so you only spend time reviewing apartments you can afford.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide exactly how strict your maximum budget limit should be or if you want to leave room for slightly more expensive options.
questions.check: What minimum and maximum price are set?
questions.say_example: What's the most you want to pay a month? I'll cap the search there.

questions.question: Does the price filter show the requested range?
questions.why: The screen shows that the price dropdown is never opened, meaning the instruction to set a monthly rent range was completely ignored.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user receives apartment recommendations that ignore their budget constraints because the price filter was never actually applied.
questions.check: Does the price filter show the requested range?
questions.say_example: The price cap didn't take. The filter still shows any price. Setting it again.

questions.question: How many bedrooms and bathrooms do you need?
questions.why: Opening the 'Beds & baths' dropdown lets you specify your exact room requirements to ensure the search results match your living needs.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide exactly how many bedrooms and bathrooms are necessary for your living situation.
questions.check: What bed and bath counts are selected?
questions.say_example: How many bedrooms do you need? And bathrooms, if that matters.

questions.question: Is the beds and baths filter still on Any?
questions.why: The instructions specified setting the number of beds and baths, but the screen showed the filter menu being opened and closed with all selections remaining on 'Any'.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user receives irrelevant apartment listings because the agent failed to apply the requested bedroom and bathroom constraints.
questions.check: Is the beds and baths filter still on Any?
questions.say_example: The beds filter is still on Any. I set it to <2> like you asked.

questions.question: Is the home type filter set to apartments?
questions.why: The screen shows 'Any' selected under 'Home type', which will include irrelevant listings like houses and townhomes instead of just apartments.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user receives search results cluttered with irrelevant property types, wasting time evaluating non-apartment listings.
questions.check: What home types does the filter show selected?
questions.say_example: Home type was on Any, so houses were mixed in. I set it to apartments.

questions.question: Does the home type filter separate apartments from condos?
questions.why: The screen shows the 'Apartments/Condos/Co-ops' filter checked, which contradicts the explicit goal to search only for apartment buildings.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user receives listings for condos and co-ops instead of strictly apartment buildings, leading to irrelevant results.
questions.check: Does the home type filter offer apartments separately from condos?
questions.say_example: This site lumps apartments and condos into one filter. A few condos may slip through. I'll flag them when I open one.

questions.question: Is corporate housing excluded?
questions.why: The filter menu includes a checkbox for 'corporate housing', which typically refers to expensive, fully furnished short-term rentals that might clutter your results if you want a standard lease.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to filter out specialized, high-cost short-term rentals, making it harder to find standard long-term apartments.
questions.check: Is the corporate housing option checked?
questions.say_example: Corporate housing not excluded.

questions.question: Which pet filters match the pets you have?
questions.why: Choosing specific pet policies like 'Allows large dogs' and 'Allows cats' immediately updates the available rentals count to ensure you only see accommodating properties.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to specify exactly which types of pets you have, potentially resulting in an agent showing you listings that do not accommodate your animals.
questions.check: Which pet policy options does the filter list, and which are selected?
questions.say_example: Do you have pets? What kind matters here. Some buildings only take cats, some cap dog weight.

questions.question: Is the no-pets filter selected?
questions.why: The pet filter includes a 'No pets allowed' option, which is crucial for renters with severe allergies or those who prefer a pet-free environment.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to ensure your future home is free of animal allergens or noise, as the agent might only focus on whether your own pets are allowed.
questions.check: Is the no-pets-allowed option available?
questions.say_example: The no-pets-allowed filter exists. Not used.

questions.question: Is the 3D tour filter selected?
questions.why: The 'More Filters' menu includes a checkbox for 'Must have 3D Tour', which allows you to only view apartments you can virtually walk through.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to prioritize listings that offer comprehensive virtual tours, which is crucial if you are renting sight-unseen or have limited time to visit in person.
questions.check: Is the 3D tour checkbox selected?
questions.say_example: 3D tour filter not used.

questions.question: What listing freshness limit is set?
questions.why: The filter menu provides options to limit results to listings added within the last 6 hours to 5 days, which helps prioritize the newest available apartments.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Letting the agent decide means you lose control over whether to prioritize acting quickly on the freshest inventory or keeping a wider pool of older listings.
questions.check: What listing age limit is selected?
questions.say_example: Left the listing age filter off.

questions.question: Are listings without a move-in date hidden?
questions.why: The 'Availability' filter includes a checkbox to 'Hide listings with no date provided', ensuring you only see apartments that explicitly confirm they are ready when you need them.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to filter out ambiguous listings, potentially wasting time evaluating apartments that might not be available on your required timeline.
questions.check: Is the hide-listings-with-no-date box checked?
questions.say_example: Kept listings with no move-in date.

questions.question: Are listings with broker fees hidden?
questions.why: The screen provides a 'HIDE LISTINGS WITH FEES' checkbox to filter out apartments that require paying an additional broker fee.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide whether to consider apartments that require paying an upfront broker fee.
questions.check: Is the hide-listings-with-fees box checked?
questions.say_example: Hid the listings that charge broker fees.

questions.question: Do the listings in the search results actually reflect the filters you just applied?
questions.why: The search results show properties costing up to $1,425 with 0 bedrooms, contradicting the $1,000 maximum and 2+ bedroom filters set previously.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user receives apartment options that completely ignore their specified budget and size requirements.
questions.check: Do the visible results stay inside the price and bedroom filters?
questions.say_example: These results ignore the filters. A <$1,425> studio got through your <$1,000> two-bed search. Running it again.

questions.question: What sort order is applied?
questions.why: The screen displays a sorting dropdown with options like 'Newest' and 'Payment (Low to High)' that determine which of the 510 properties you will see and evaluate first.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide whether to prioritize the site's algorithm recommendations, the newest inventory, or the lowest prices when browsing the results.
questions.check: What sort order is selected?
questions.say_example: Sorted by price, low to high.

children.label: Survey the results
children.note: 5.1 after every change in 3 or 4. 5.2 or 5.3 by surface - list-first sites scan cards, map-first surfaces probe pins and clusters. 5.4 and 5.5 while scanning. 5.6 ends the pass; back out of 6 and re-enter 5.6 for the next candidate (pCy8, mKVE, Q8ex, iHOh).

questions.question: Should you continue with a truncated export of 1,000 listings, or close the dialog to refine your search?
questions.why: The 'Export limit exceeded' dialog requires you to decide whether to accept an incomplete dataset of the first 1,000 listings or adjust your filters to reduce the total count.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide whether a truncated dataset is sufficient for your evaluation or if applying stricter filters is necessary to capture all relevant listings.
questions.check: Does the page show an export limit dialog, and what does it say?
questions.say_example: The export stops at 1,000 listings. I'm tightening the filters so nothing gets cut off.

questions.question: Did your search yield any results, or do you need to adjust your filters?
questions.why: The screen displayed a banner stating 'No homes match your search', indicating that the current criteria are too restrictive and need modification.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to decide exactly which search criteria to relax or change when no initial results are found.
questions.check: Does the page say no homes match the search?
questions.say_example: Nothing matches in <Sturbridge> at that price. I can widen the area, or raise the cap. Which one?

questions.question: Did the platform silently drop your strict filters to show 'similar' results?
questions.why: When a search yields zero exact matches, many apartment sites automatically remove strict filters (like budget caps or pet policies) to show 'nearby' or 'similar' listings without a prominent warning.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You end up evaluating apartments that are too expensive or do not allow your pets because you falsely assumed your filters were still active.
questions.check: Does the results page say filters were removed or that it is showing similar or nearby listings?
questions.say_example: Careful, the site quietly dropped your pet filter to pad out the list. Some of these won't take <your dog>. Re-filtering.

questions.question: How many listings match the current filters?
questions.why: Seeing the 1,228 total results and map clusters like '25+' or '50+' helps you decide if your filters are too broad or if you should zoom in on a specific neighborhood.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to visually gauge which specific neighborhoods have the highest concentration of available apartments within your budget.
questions.check: How many results does the header say match?
questions.say_example: Found <1,228> places with your filters. Most sit around <downtown>.

questions.question: Are you accurately reading the total number of available rentals in the results header?
questions.why: The screen clearly displays '8 rentals available' and shows three property cards, so falsely claiming there is only one rental misrepresents the search results.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses an accurate picture of market availability and might miss out on viable apartments if the agent artificially limits the options.
questions.check: How many rentals does the results header say are available?
questions.say_example: The page actually says <8> rentals, so there are more options than I said.

questions.question: Should you skip the featured listings at the top and select an organic result?
questions.why: The top two listings are marked as featured paid placements and lack square footage data, while the first organic listing clearly displays its size.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to bypass paid promotions and prioritize organic listings that provide complete information like square footage.
questions.check: Which results are labelled Featured, Sponsored, or Ad?
questions.say_example: The top two are paid placements, so I'm starting below them.

questions.question: Should you view any of the nearby listings outside the Moundville boundary, or stop evaluating?
questions.why: The screen indicates there are no more exact matches in Moundville but shows seven nearby rentals, requiring a choice on whether to consider properties outside the original boundary.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide if living in a nearby town is an acceptable compromise for finding a suitable apartment.
questions.check: Does the page say there are no more exact matches, and how many nearby listings does it offer?
questions.say_example: Only <one> exact match in <Moundville>. There are <seven> more just outside the line. Want me to include those?

questions.question: Which listing should you select from the search results based on your budget and requirements?
questions.why: The search results display multiple listings with varying rents, sizes, and room counts, requiring you to weigh these details to find the best match.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means losing the ability to personally weigh the trade-offs between rent, size, and specific apartment features when choosing a candidate.
questions.check: What price, beds, and location does each shortlisted card show?
questions.say_example: Two good ones under <$2,000>. <The Marlowe>, <$1,850>, two beds, cats OK, <10 minutes> from work. <Horizons North>, <$1,795>, but a <40 minute> drive. Which one?

children.label: Vet the listing
children.note: 6.1 to 6.9 in any order and depth - most keepers read two or three and skip the rest. 6.3 wherever the page is held against the card that promised it. 6.10 where money is the question. exit to 5 for another candidate, to 7 to make contact, or to 8 to keep it - mKVE rejects a listing on 6.2 alone, n9qo on 6.5.

questions.question: What extra tabs does the listing page offer?
questions.why: The top navigation includes tabs for 'Facts & features' and 'Neighborhood' that provide crucial context and structured data not found on the default overview.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the assurance that the agent fully evaluated the property's complete profile, potentially causing them to skip a suitable apartment based on incomplete information.
questions.check: What tabs does the listing page show?
questions.say_example: Read the facts and neighborhood tabs.

questions.question: What availability date and time on market does the listing state?
questions.why: Checking details like the November 30th availability, the four days on the market, and the luxury description ensures the apartment is a viable candidate before you commit to it.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to explicitly verify the specific amenities further down the page, relying instead on the agent's trust in the initial search filters and general description.
questions.check: What availability date and days on market does the listing state?
questions.say_example: Available <Nov 30>, on the market <4 days>.

questions.question: Does the lease term in the description match the asked-for term?
questions.why: Although the search result had a 'Furnished' tag, the detailed description revealed it was actually an unfurnished short-term lease ending in April.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the stability of a long-term home if the agent ignores the description and commits you to a short-term lease that forces an early move.
questions.check: What lease term does the description state?
questions.say_example: The lease here ends in <April>. You asked for a full year. I'd let this one go.

questions.question: Does the listing description contain common scam red flags, such as asking for a deposit before a tour or stating the owner is out of the country?
questions.why: Scam listings often have prices that are too good to be true and descriptions that demand upfront wire transfers or explain why the landlord cannot meet in person.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You risk handing over personal information or money to a fraudulent lister because the agent only checked the price and bedroom count.
questions.check: Does the description ask for money before a tour, or say the owner is out of the country?
questions.say_example: This one wants a deposit before you ever see the place. And the owner is supposedly out of the country. That's how the scams read. I'd skip it.

questions.question: Does the description explicitly state that the photos show a 'model unit' or 'similar apartment' rather than the actual unit for rent?
questions.why: Large apartment complexes often use photos of staged, renovated model units that look significantly better than the specific apartment actually available to lease.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user might waste time touring or applying for an apartment expecting luxury finishes, only to find the actual unit is outdated or has a different layout.
questions.check: Does the description say the photos show a model unit or a similar apartment?
questions.say_example: The photos are of a model unit. The one for rent may look worse.

children.label: Check the page against the card

questions.question: Does the advertised starting price on the search result match the actual rent of the cheapest available unit?
questions.why: Verifying that the search card's '$3,879+ Studio' matches Unit 3B's actual base rent ensures the listing is accurate and not using deceptive pricing.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to personally verify that the advertised price accurately reflects the actual available units rather than a bait-and-switch tactic.
questions.check: What starting price did the card show, and what is the cheapest unit on the page?
questions.say_example: The card said from <$3,879>. The cheapest real unit is <$4,210>. The teaser price doesn't exist right now.

questions.question: Do the bedroom and bathroom counts in the description match the listing header?
questions.why: The listing header displayed 4 beds and 4 baths, but the property description contradicted this by claiming 3 bedrooms and 3 baths.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the chance to catch glaring inconsistencies that might indicate a scam or an apartment that doesn't actually fit their needs.
questions.check: What bed and bath counts do the header and the description each state?
questions.say_example: The header says <4> bedrooms. The description says <3>. One of them is wrong, so I'll ask which before you decide.

questions.question: Does the description's furnished status match the tag on the card?
questions.why: The search results previewed the apartment as furnished, but the detailed description explicitly stated it was an unfurnished short-term lease.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user might waste time inquiring about an unfurnished apartment when they actually needed a furnished one.
questions.check: Does the description's furnished status match the tag on the card?
questions.say_example: The card had a furnished tag. The description says it comes empty. Don't count on furniture.

questions.question: Does the move-in special advertised on the search results page match the one on the detailed property page?
questions.why: Inconsistent move-in specials between the search results and the detailed property page could indicate misleading advertising or affect the actual cost.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to verify the exact terms of the move-in special, potentially leading to unexpected costs or missed savings.
questions.check: Does the move-in special on the card appear on the listing page?
questions.say_example: The card promised <a month free>. The listing page never mentions it. Don't count on the discount.

questions.question: Does the address on the page match the location named in the listing title?
questions.why: The street view showed the building number as [address], which contradicted the listing's text of [address] and suggests a potential scam or inaccurate listing.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the critical visual verification that ensures the property actually exists at the advertised location, risking engagement with a fraudulent listing.
questions.check: Does the street address on the page match the place named in the listing title?
questions.say_example: The listing calls itself <Redwood City>. The address is really in <San Carlos>, across the freeway.

questions.question: Does the actual monthly cost on the detail page match the advertised price from the search results?
questions.why: The initial search result quoted a base price of $1,270, but the property detail page disclosed additional non-optional fees and utilities that increase the true monthly cost.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user might waste time touring or applying for an apartment that ultimately exceeds their budget because the agent ignored hidden fees.
questions.check: What monthly total do the page's required fees add up to, against the advertised price?
questions.say_example: The real monthly cost is <$1,410> once the required fees go in. That's <$140> over the advertised price.

questions.question: Does the description say the price is for a room rather than the whole unit?
questions.why: The listing header advertises $900 for 4 beds, but the tags and description explicitly state it is only a room for rent.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user wastes time inquiring about a shared room situation when they expected to rent an entire apartment.
questions.check: Does the description say the price is for a room rather than the whole unit?
questions.say_example: That <$900> rents a single room. The other <three> bedrooms come with housemates.

questions.question: Is the estimated monthly payment consistent between the comparable homes carousel and the property details page?
questions.why: The comparable homes carousel listed the payment as $1,028/mo, but the property details page showed $937/mo.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses accurate financial expectations if the agent fails to notice conflicting pricing information.
questions.check: What monthly payment estimates appear on the page, and do they agree?
questions.say_example: Two payment estimates on the page disagree, <$1,028> and <$937>.

questions.question: Is the listing marked as 'Pending' or 'Application Submitted' in the description, despite showing as 'Available' in the search results?
questions.why: Property managers often leave listings active to collect backup applications, but note in the description that an application is already pending.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user wastes an application fee and time applying for an apartment that is already effectively taken.
questions.check: Does the description say an application is pending or submitted?
questions.say_example: The description says an application is already in on this one. It may be gone before you could apply.

questions.question: Do the available floor plan sizes match the square footage range advertised in the property summary?
questions.why: Verifying the specific floor plans ensures you are not misled by a broad summary range that doesn't reflect the actual units shown on screen.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses accurate expectations about the apartment size if the agent relies on a misleading summary range instead of verifying the actual available units.
questions.check: What sizes do the floor plans list, against the range in the summary?
questions.say_example: The summary promised up to <1,100> square feet. The biggest unit listed is <850>.

questions.question: Which specific floorplan and unit should you choose?
questions.why: The screen lists multiple available units within the building, such as '7K' and '6C', with varying prices and square footage.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to personally weigh the trade-offs between specific unit prices, layouts, and square footage before starting the application.
questions.check: What units does the availability table list, with price, size, and date?
questions.say_example: Two units work here. <7K>, <$2,150>, <720> square feet, free <June 1>. <6C>, <$2,090>, a floor lower. Which one?

questions.question: Are you eligible for this specific community based on its age or income restrictions?
questions.why: The listing is explicitly tagged as 'Senior housing' and 'Income restricted', meaning you must meet specific age and financial criteria to legally rent there.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user wastes time evaluating or applying for an apartment they are legally or financially disqualified from renting.
questions.check: Is the listing tagged senior housing or income restricted?
questions.say_example: This building is seniors only, <62> and up. You can't rent it, so I'm moving on.

questions.question: Does the description list specific pet breed or weight restrictions that the general 'Pets Allowed' filter missed?
questions.why: The broad 'Pets Allowed' filter often includes properties that only allow cats or have strict 15-lb weight limits, which are only disclosed deep in the written description.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user might fall in love with a listing and initiate contact, only to be rejected later because their specific dog breed or size is prohibited by the fine print.
questions.check: Does the description state pet breed or weight limits?
questions.say_example: Pets are allowed here, but only under <15 pounds>. <Rex> is over the limit, so this one's out.

questions.question: What does the price history table show?
questions.why: The price history table reveals past fluctuations and listing events, which, along with the Rent Zestimate, helps determine if the current asking price is fair.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally judge whether the current rent is a good deal based on its historical price changes and market benchmarks.
questions.check: What price changes does the history table show?
questions.say_example: Price history shows a <$2,700> drop in <March>.

questions.question: Does the listed rent match the lower price in the price history?
questions.why: Checking the price history ensures the current rent of $24,800 correctly includes the recent $2,700 decrease from the previous $27,500 listing price.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses valuable financial context about the property's recent price drop, which could be crucial for evaluating the deal or negotiating the lease.
questions.check: Does the current rent match the latest price in the history table?
questions.say_example: The history says the rent dropped to <$24,800>. The listing still shows <$27,500>. I'll trust the higher number until they confirm.

questions.question: What Walk and Transit scores does the page show?
questions.why: The screen shows extremely low Walk, Transit, and Bike scores, meaning you will need a car for almost all daily activities.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to decide if you are willing to compromise on walkability and transit access for this specific apartment.
questions.check: What Walk, Transit, and Bike scores does the page show?
questions.say_example: The Walk Score here is <0>. You'd need a car for everything, even groceries.

questions.question: Is the listing price realistic compared to the neighborhood median?
questions.why: Comparing the $2,025 listing price to the $2,250 neighborhood median confirms the deal is realistic and not a suspiciously cheap scam.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to apply your own judgment on whether a below-market price is a lucky find or a red flag for a scam.
questions.check: What is the listing price, and what neighborhood median does the page show?
questions.say_example: This one is <$500> under the going rate nearby. Deals that big usually have a catch. I'm reading the fine print before we trust it.

questions.question: What additional services does the company list?
questions.why: The screen shows the company offers extra conveniences like online room tours, digital contracts, and free utility setup, which might influence your choice of listing.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to prioritize a company that provides specific conveniences like online contracts or utility setup that best fit your personal needs.
questions.check: What extra services does the company page list?
questions.say_example: The company offers online tours and free utility setup.

questions.question: What office address and hours does the page state?
questions.why: Reviewing the physical address, transit access, and operating hours helps you verify the agency's legitimacy and determine if you can easily visit them.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally assess whether the office's location and operating hours are convenient for your own schedule.
questions.check: What office address and hours does the page state?
questions.say_example: Office at <the address shown>, open <weekdays 9 to 6>.

questions.question: Do the business hours shown in the contact modal agree with the office page?
questions.why: The contact modal lists weekday-only hours while the office page claims they are open every day, revealing a contradiction in the listing's details.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You might attempt to contact the agent or schedule a tour on a weekend when the office is actually closed.
questions.check: Do the hours in the contact modal match the office page?
questions.say_example: The contact box and the office page disagree on hours.

questions.question: What track record does the agent profile show?
questions.why: Checking the agent's profile for past rentals and sales helps confirm you are dealing with a legitimate broker rather than a potential scammer.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the peace of mind that comes from personally verifying a broker's track record and online reputation before reaching out.
questions.check: What past rentals and sales does the agent profile list?
questions.say_example: The agent's profile shows <34> past rentals.

questions.question: What are the promotion terms and the base rent?
questions.why: Calculating the actual value of the 'Two Months Free' offer against the $1,270 base rent ensures the promotion provides the expected $2,540 minimum savings.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the assurance that the advertised move-in specials actually translate to the expected financial savings.
questions.check: What does the promotion say, and what is the base rent?
questions.say_example: The two months free checks out against the <$1,270> rent.

children.label: Work out the true cost
children.note: 6.11.1 and 6.11.2 as the page surfaces them; 6.11.3 leaves the site for a calculator (dRfh). the answer can end the search - dRfh prices move-in at double the rent before contacting anyone.

questions.question: What monthly and move-in costs does the breakdown list?
questions.why: The screen shows significant additional expenses like agency and guarantor fees that drastically increase the initial move-in cost beyond just the base rent.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to weigh whether the high upfront move-in fees fit your personal budget before committing to an inquiry.
questions.check: What monthly and one-time costs does the fee breakdown list?
questions.say_example: The real move-in cost here is <$5,400> once the deposit and fees go in. Monthly it's <$2,150> with the building fees.

questions.question: What additional fees apply to this base rent?
questions.why: The listing explicitly states 'Fees may apply' next to the base rent, indicating that the advertised price does not include all mandatory monthly or upfront costs.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user might commit to touring or applying for an apartment without realizing that hidden fees push the actual cost over their budget.
questions.check: Does the page say fees may apply without listing the amounts?
questions.say_example: The price says fees may apply, and never says how much. I'll ask them for the true monthly total.

questions.question: Is the price being compared the base rent, or the total monthly price with the move-in specials and fees folded in?
questions.why: The interface features a 'Total monthly price' toggle that automatically factors in move-in specials and fees, giving a more accurate picture of the actual monthly cost.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to instantly see the true amortized cost of the apartment, forcing them to manually calculate the value of any free rent promotions.
questions.check: Is there a total monthly price toggle, and what total does it show?
questions.say_example: Used the total monthly price toggle.

questions.question: What income requirement does the listing state?
questions.why: Calculating that you need $152,000 in annual income for the $3,800 rent ensures you only spend time inquiring about apartments you actually qualify for.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to personally verify if their specific financial situation meets the strict income requirements for the apartment.
questions.check: What income requirement does the listing state?
questions.say_example: This one wants proof you earn <40> times the rent. That's <$152,000> a year here.

questions.question: Does the stated income requirement match the rent times the multiple the page names?
questions.why: The calculator needs to display the result of multiplying the $3,800 monthly rent by 40 to verify the required annual income.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the assurance that the income requirement for the apartment was accurately calculated and verified.
questions.check: Does the income figure shown equal the rent times the stated multiple?
questions.say_example: The math on the page is off. <$3,800> times <40> is <$152,000>, and they show <$142,000>.

children.label: Contact the property
children.note: 7.1 opens the form - or ends the goal when both buttons are read and left alone (cd07, iHOh). 7.2 to 7.4 in the order the form asks. 7.5 ends it, and in this corpus always by closing: ten keepers reach a form, none sends.

questions.question: Did a CAPTCHA or security challenge appear that needs to be solved before the inquiry can actually be sent?
questions.why: Listing sites frequently use CAPTCHAs to prevent bot spam on their contact forms, which can silently block a submission if not completed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The inquiry is never actually sent to the landlord because the agent failed to notice or solve the anti-bot challenge.
questions.check: Is a CAPTCHA or security challenge blocking the form?
questions.say_example: There's a robot check I can't pass. Can you tap the box for me?

questions.question: Does the confirmation email match what you asked for?
questions.why: Reviewing the confirmation email ensures that the correct parameters, such as your contact info and requested tour time, were successfully submitted to the property.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally verify that the correct contact information and viewing preferences were sent to the landlord.
questions.check: Do the details in the confirmation email match the request that was sent?
questions.say_example: The confirmation email doesn't match what we sent. It shows <Tuesday>, and we asked for <Saturday>. I'll follow up.

questions.question: Does the page confirm the request was sent?
questions.why: The screen displayed a pop-up modal with a checkmark and success message, which is the only way to guarantee the inquiry was actually processed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the immediate peace of mind of seeing the visual confirmation that their specific message successfully went through to the property manager.
questions.check: Does the page show a success message for the inquiry?
questions.say_example: Sent. The site confirmed your request to <Origin Apartments> at <3:07>.

questions.question: Did the confirmation message state that the property manager will contact you, or does it require you to call them to confirm the tour?
questions.why: A 'success' screen might actually contain instructions that the user must take further action, like calling a number, to actually secure the booking.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user thinks the tour is booked, but it gets canceled because they didn't see the instruction to call and confirm.
questions.check: Does the confirmation say the property will contact you, or that you must call?
questions.say_example: The confirmation says you have to call them to lock in the tour. Nothing is booked until that call.

questions.question: Did the confirmation screen include a visual upsell for a paid renter profile or background check that you should ignore?
questions.why: After a successful inquiry, platforms often display prominent visual upsells for premium services, which can look like required next steps if not read carefully.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user might be tricked into paying for an unnecessary premium renter profile or background check because the agent mistook the visual upsell for a mandatory application step.
questions.check: Does the screen after the inquiry offer a paid profile or background check?
questions.say_example: The next screen is selling a paid renter profile. You don't need it for this. I'm skipping past it.

questions.question: Should you plan to attend the scheduled open house instead of requesting a private tour?
questions.why: The listing displays an upcoming open house on Sunday from 1-4pm, offering a chance to view the property without needing to schedule an appointment.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to simply walk into the open house, potentially missing out if the agent waits for a private tour response that comes too late.
questions.check: Does the listing show open house times?
questions.say_example: There's an open house <Sunday, 1 to 4>. You could just walk in. Want that instead of booking a tour?

questions.question: Do you want to request a tour or request to apply for this property?
questions.why: The screen presents both a blue 'Request a tour' button and a white 'Request to apply' button, which initiate very different steps in the rental process.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide whether you want to view the property in person first or immediately commit to starting the application process.
questions.check: What contact buttons does the listing offer?
questions.say_example: Should I ask for a tour, or start an application? Applying usually costs a fee and runs a credit check.

questions.question: Is the inquiry type set to renting?
questions.why: The dropdown menu presents different contact methods that determine whether you send a standard message or request a specialized tour.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide the specific type of purchasing inquiry or tour experience you want to initiate.
questions.check: Which inquiry type is selected in the dropdown?
questions.say_example: The form was set to buying. I switched it to renting.

questions.question: Does the disclaimer say this form goes to someone other than the lister?
questions.why: The disclaimer warns that inquiries about property requests should only go to the person listed in the property details, meaning this general contact form might be the wrong channel.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose control over the exact wording of the inquiry and the chance to notice if the form's disclaimer invalidates your request.
questions.check: What does the disclaimer under the form say about who receives the inquiry?
questions.say_example: The fine print says this form doesn't reach the landlord. I'm using the contact on the listing instead.

questions.question: Did clicking 'Request a tour' open a scheduling form, or did it redirect you to an external property management website?
questions.why: Aggregator sites often link out to third-party portals for the actual booking, which means the process and required information will suddenly change.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent might fail the task if it doesn't realize it has been redirected and needs to navigate a completely new website to finish the request.
questions.check: Did the tour button open a form here, or a different website?
questions.say_example: The tour button jumped to the building's own site. The form there asks for different things. I'll keep going and tell you if it wants more.

questions.question: What should the message say?
questions.why: The pop-up form requires a phone number to proceed and provides a default message that can be customized.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to personalize the inquiry or ask specific questions before submitting the tour request.
questions.check: What fields and message does the form require before sending?
questions.say_example: Here's what I'll send. You'd like a tour <Saturday morning> for unit <7K>, and a question about parking. Anything to add before I write it in?

questions.question: Are all fields in the request form filled out correctly without errors?
questions.why: The phone number field shows a red border and a 'Please enter a valid phone number' error, which will prevent the request from being sent.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to contact the property because the agent fails to provide a valid phone number to successfully submit the form.
questions.check: Does any form field show a validation error?
questions.say_example: The form flagged the phone number. I'm fixing the format and trying again.

questions.question: Does the form show an availability notice that conflicts with the ask?
questions.why: The form includes a notice that only one-room apartments are currently available, which might affect your decision to proceed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The ability to decide whether to continue applying given the restriction to one-room apartments.
questions.check: Does the form show a notice about limited availability?
questions.say_example: The form says only one-room flats are left. Your two-bedroom ask won't be met here. Still want me to send?

questions.question: Which personal fields is the form asking for?
questions.why: The form includes mandatory fields like your name and phone number, alongside optional fields like your current address that you must decide whether to share.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide exactly which optional personal details are shared with the listing agent.
questions.check: Which fields are required, and which are optional?
questions.say_example: I'm filling in your name, email, and phone number. The address field is optional, so I'm leaving it blank.

questions.question: Do you have a housing entitlement certificate (WBS)?
questions.why: The inquiry form requires you to indicate whether you hold a WBS certificate to determine your eligibility for the apartment.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to accurately report your housing entitlement status, which could result in your inquiry being rejected if the agent guesses incorrectly.
questions.check: Does the form ask for a WBS housing certificate?
questions.say_example: The form asks if you hold a WBS certificate. That's the German housing permit, and this flat needs one. Do you have it?

questions.question: Who should you address in your inquiry message?
questions.why: Identifying the specific contact person shown on the listing, such as [provider], ensures your message is properly directed and professional.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personalize the greeting and carefully set the tone of your initial communication with the property manager.
questions.check: Which contact name does the listing show?
questions.say_example: Addressed the message to <[name]>.

questions.question: Which unique property identifier should you include in the inquiry template?
questions.why: Copying the specific Object ID from the listing's overview ensures the property manager knows exactly which unit you are inquiring about.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the certainty that the exact property identifier is correctly referenced in your personalized inquiry message.
questions.check: What object ID does the listing overview show?
questions.say_example: Included object ID <B-2231> in the message.

questions.question: What is the exact address to include in your inquiry template?
questions.why: The top of the listing page displays the full property address, which needs to be accurately copied into your message so the landlord knows which specific unit you are referencing.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to verify that the correct property address was accurately extracted and included in your outreach message.
questions.check: What full address does the listing page show?
questions.say_example: Included the full address in the message.

questions.question: What income source and bracket does the form require you to select?
questions.why: The inquiry form requires you to select your income source from options like salary, unemployment, or retirement to qualify for the apartment.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might select an incorrect income type, which could lead to your inquiry being rejected by the property manager.
questions.check: What income questions does the form require?
questions.say_example: The form wants your income source and your monthly range before it will send. What should I put in?

questions.question: Does the message name the unit that was chosen?
questions.why: The main contact form on a building's listing page often sends a generic inquiry to the leasing office without automatically indicating which specific unit or floorplan you expanded and evaluated.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user risks the landlord assuming they are interested in a different, potentially more expensive unit, or receiving a generic auto-reply instead of information about the specific apartment they want.
questions.check: Does the message name the exact unit that was chosen?
questions.say_example: The message didn't name a unit, so I added <7K>. Now they know which one you mean.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of your inquiry?
questions.why: The contact form includes a 'Purpose of inquiry' dropdown with options like 'I want to know availability', which sets the context for the agent receiving your message.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to explicitly categorize your request, potentially leading to slower or less relevant responses from the leasing agent.
questions.check: What purpose options does the inquiry dropdown list?
questions.say_example: Set the inquiry purpose to availability.

questions.question: Is the marketing-email box pre-checked?
questions.why: The contact form includes a pre-checked box to 'Email me listings and apartment related info', which will subscribe you to marketing communications if left checked.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose control over your inbox, potentially receiving unwanted promotional emails and alerts because the agent failed to uncheck the marketing opt-in.
questions.check: Which consent boxes are pre-checked?
questions.say_example: Said no to marketing emails.

questions.question: Are any pre-checked boxes consenting to share details with third parties?
questions.why: Many listing aggregators monetize inquiries by pre-checking consent boxes that allow them to sell your phone number and email to moving companies, insurers, or mortgage brokers.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You end up receiving relentless spam calls and emails from third parties because the agent didn't uncheck the hidden marketing consent boxes.
questions.check: Are any pre-checked boxes about sharing details with third parties?
questions.say_example: A box was already ticked to share your number with movers and insurers. I unticked it.

questions.question: What does the form say the application checkbox does?
questions.why: The 'Request Application' checkbox merely adds a line to your initial inquiry email asking the landlord for next steps; it does not actually initiate or log a formal rental application in the platform's 'My Applications' portal.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user might falsely believe they have successfully applied for the apartment and wait for a status update in their account, ultimately missing out on the property because they never completed the actual application process.
questions.check: What does the form say the application checkbox actually does?
questions.say_example: That application checkbox only adds a line to the email. It doesn't start a real application anywhere.

questions.question: Do you want to send the pre-filled inquiry message to the agent?
questions.why: The screen displays a pre-filled email to the broker, requiring a choice to either send the inquiry or cancel it.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An AI might automatically send the generic message, removing your ability to customize the text or back out of the inquiry.
questions.check: What does the form show it is about to send, and to whom?
questions.say_example: Ready to send. A tour request for <the Marlowe, unit 7K>, <Saturday morning>, with your name and phone number. Send it, or say change.

questions.question: Does the fine print include consent to calls and texts from affiliates?
questions.why: Submitting the tour request form includes a disclaimer that you consent to receive calls and texts from the platform's affiliates and real estate agents, which could lead to unwanted phone solicitations.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user inadvertently consents to receiving spam calls and text messages from real estate agents because the browser agent accepted the hidden terms without asking.
questions.check: Does the fine print consent to calls and texts from affiliates?
questions.say_example: Sending this also agrees to calls and texts from their partner agents. Expect a few calls this week.

questions.question: Does submitting the tour request form include fine print consenting to a soft credit check or background screening?
questions.why: Some aggressive leasing platforms embed consent for preliminary credit or background checks directly into the initial contact or tour scheduling form.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user might unknowingly have their credit profiled or personal data run through a screening service before they even decide if they like the property.
questions.check: Does the fine print consent to a credit or background check?
questions.say_example: Careful, the fine print here runs a credit check just for the tour request. That mark outlives the request. Still want to send?

questions.question: Does the page show the form submitted?
questions.why: The video cuts away while the 'Property Inquiry' form is still blank, meaning the contact step was never completed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user misses out on actually contacting the property because the inquiry was never sent.
questions.check: Does the page show the form submitted, or still blank?
questions.say_example: The form never went through. It's still sitting blank. I'm filling it in again.

children.label: Save listings and searches
children.note: each of 8.1 to 8.5 where the keeper wants something durable - 8.1 fires from three surfaces: the results card (TNMH), the map preview (cd07), the detail page (pCy8). 8.2 reaches into 2.5 when signed out (dS5q). 8.6 after a save; 8.7 as its own tour of the account.

questions.question: Which listings were saved to favorites?
questions.why: The feed displays multiple options with varying prices and locations, such as a $2,[address] and a $4,895 unit on E 13th St, so you must decide which ones are worth saving.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to apply your subjective preferences for specific streets and price points when curating a shortlist of potential homes.
questions.check: Which listings does the feed show, with price and location?
questions.say_example: Saved <2> listings to favorites.

questions.question: Which folder was the listing saved to?
questions.why: The screen shows a save modal for the '[address] 82nd Street' rental that requires selecting a specific folder like '[name]' to organize the listing.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to organize their favorite apartment candidates into specific custom folders for later review.
questions.check: What folders does the save modal list?
questions.say_example: Saved it to the <apartment hunt> folder.

questions.question: Does the page show the search saved?
questions.why: The narrator explicitly asked to save the search, but the cursor only hovered over the button without clicking it, meaning the search parameters won't be saved for later.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to easily return to or receive alerts for this specific set of apartment filters because the search was never actually saved.
questions.check: Does the page show the search as saved?
questions.say_example: The search never actually saved. I'm clicking it properly this time.

questions.question: Is the search saved for alerts?
questions.why: The search results list includes a 'Save my search' prompt to 'See new homes first,' offering a way to receive future alerts for these specific filters.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide whether you want to receive ongoing notifications and emails about new properties that match this search.
questions.check: Does the page offer to save the search for alerts?
questions.say_example: I saved this search, so new matches will come to you first.

questions.question: Which neighborhoods are selected for alerts?
questions.why: The map overlay allows selecting multiple adjacent neighborhoods like West Village and Tribeca to customize the alert feed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to hand-pick the exact neighborhoods you are willing to live in.
questions.check: Which neighborhoods are selected on the alert map?
questions.say_example: Alerts set for <West Village> and <Tribeca>, same as the search.

questions.question: What are the exact parameters of your saved search, and how many recently updated results are available to view?
questions.why: The screen displays a detailed string of your applied filters, such as price range and amenities, alongside quick links to view all 25 rentals or just the 9 updated in the last week.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to verify that the saved search criteria perfectly match your specific requirements before time is spent evaluating individual listings.
questions.check: What filter summary does the saved search show?
questions.say_example: Saved search reads <$1,500 to $2,000, 2 beds, cats>.

questions.question: Does the saved search match the filters you picked?
questions.why: Checking the auto-generated search summary ensures the platform correctly captured all your specific requirements for price, location, and amenities.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to verify that the system correctly interpreted and saved your exact housing requirements.
questions.check: Does the saved search summary include every filter that was set?
questions.say_example: The saved search dropped your pet filter. I put it back so the alerts match what you asked.

questions.question: Does the number of saved listings match the ones you actually favorited?
questions.why: The Favorites badge count incorrectly jumps from 1 to 3 after saving just one additional listing, and an unselected $4,365 apartment mysteriously appears in the folder.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose control over your curated options if the agent silently adds unselected, expensive listings to your favorites.
questions.check: Do the listings in the favorites folder match the ones that were saved?
questions.say_example: Your favorites show <three> saves, and you only picked <two>. The site slipped a promoted one in. I'm removing it.

questions.question: What label does the saved listing carry in the alerts feed, and what label in favorites?
questions.why: The screen showed the $4,895 E 13th St listing labeled as '4h' in the alerts feed but 'Featured' in favorites, which matters because it might indicate a promoted listing rather than a genuinely new one.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to spot inconsistencies in listing labels that might reveal a property is a paid promotion rather than a fresh market opportunity.
questions.check: What labels does the saved listing carry in the alerts feed and in favorites?
questions.say_example: The <E 13th St> save now shows a Featured tag.

questions.question: What listings appear under Messaged Listings?
questions.why: Checking the 'Messaged Listings' screen allows you to track specific properties like [address] and [address] that you have already contacted.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this means you lose the ability to personally verify and keep track of exactly which apartments have already received your inquiries.
questions.check: Which listings does the messaged page list?
questions.say_example: You've messaged <2> places so far.

questions.question: Are there any current messages in your inbox?
questions.why: The screen explicitly displays a 'No Messages' state, confirming whether there is any existing or pending communication with property managers.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the situational awareness of knowing their communication history is currently empty before initiating or verifying new apartment inquiries.
questions.check: Does the inbox show any messages?
questions.say_example: No replies yet.

questions.question: What does the My Applications page show?
questions.why: The 'My Applications' page displays 'No Applications Yet', which serves as the definitive record of whether your application was successfully processed by the platform.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally verify that your application was successfully registered and tracked in your account.
questions.check: What does the applications page show?
questions.say_example: The applications page shows none on file. The inquiry went by email only.
